title: “Mechanical Motion”: Frame Rates and Repeated Patterns (Prelude, Fugue, and Postlude No.4, Book II)
content_blocks: When I was a kid watching old movies on Channel 9 or 11, I was always fascinated by the way that as a car would start its wheels (or the propellers of a plane) would slowly accelerate, would then seem to stop, and then start to spin backward. The propellers in the first minute of this film show how propellers can seem to spin backwards, forwards, or barely move at all (the helicopter rotors on this and this video are even stranger, matching the frame rate of the camera so perfectly that they look immobile).

This is precisely the way the fugue from this trio of pieces works:  an upward moving scalar pattern in one hand is set against the same pattern—inverted—in the other.  Both lines accelerate, but given the “frame rate” of nine notes per second it sounds first as accelerations and then again creates the illusion of slowing down in both lines.  Meanwhile, the upward moving line (again, because of the “frame rate”—or what we could call “quantization”) seems to invert, as the notes that are 10, 11, 12 notes apart in the pattern create a downward-moving pattern.  We soon realize that the upward moving line was not actually an inversion of the original, downward moving line, but a quantization of a different rotating speed of the same material—a two-voice fugue with different tempi.  As a little joke, the piece begins with an accelerating series of percussive notes meant to evoke the flicker sound of old-time film projectors; as the film runs out at the end, the percussive notes return, decelerating.

The composition—the working out—of the fugue is one thing, but really it wouldn’t work without the piano preparations.  All of the notes in the left hand are played on strings with poster putty placed at the octave node, generating harmonics an octave higher—which thus place them in precisely the same register as the right-hand notes.  The result is almost a cubist vision of two different perspectives of the same material.  (The percussive film projector sounds come from upper-register notes that are dampened so that no pitch comes through, leaving just the wooden-sounding drum-like sounds.)

The prelude is similar, except that rather than two voices in counterpoint, it is one voice with multiple recursive—fractal—embeddings of itself, at different rates. Each note of the slowest-moving embedding of the melody thus spawns a somewhat faster version of the same melody, and in turn each of those notes spawns a somewhat faster version of the same melody, etc.—in effect, a fugue, in which the different fugal voices start at the same time but at different rates There are a total of four or five fractal layers in this piece; as the notes move toward the end of each of their embedded melodies the spaces between the notes enlarge, better enabling us to hear the sparkling and subtle variations in sound quality that result from the preparations.

Lastly, there is a postlude to this set (unique in both books of preludes and fugues).  In the postlude it is the individual notes of the scale that occur at different rates or quantizations, creating an impression of a particular pattern of particles spinning slowly in space.
Michael Mizrahi’s stunning performance of these pieces can be heard online: Prelude, Fugue, and Postlude.
